newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish bonds ease back amid French poll fears.
newsitem.headline: Irish bonds ease back amid French poll fears.

text.p: Irish bonds eased back in line with other European bond markets on Wednesday amid rumours of a private poll showing the French socialists on course to win the parliamentary election on Sunday, dealers said.
"The uncertainty surrounding the French election is again the factor hurting European markets today," a dealer said. "The Irish market is showing nerves along with everyone else."
However, the dealer added, on spreads the peripheral markets, Ireland included, did not seem to be too badly hit, and volume in the Irish market was "reasonable".
By 1510 GMT the 6.5 percent bond due 2001 was down two pence at 101.98 to yield 5.96 percent, while the eight percent bond due 2006 was down 17 pence at 108.55 to yield 6.72 percent.

Dealers said that yields against German bunds had tightened marginally from the previous close, with the yield against Germany at 139 basis points over in the five-year bond, and 86 over in the 10-year.

Rumours on Wednesday that private opinion polls were showing the French socialists in line for a win spooked the markets because of fears the left-wing party will be less willing to make sacrifices to achieve European monetary union.
The long end of the curve was hit as expectations were raised of a softer euro with more countries in the first wave should the French socialists win.
Dealers said the reduced inflation forecasts in yesterday's annual report from the Irish Central Bank had benefitted the short end of the curve.

Also, an opinion poll this morning showing Ireland's opposition parties maintaining a lead over the government in the run-up to the country's general election on June 6 had not had any immediate impact in the market, dealers said.

"The possible results of the election are not fully priced into the market yet," a dealer said. "Despite the polls up to now, a hung parliament is a real possibility, and that would be the worst scenario for us."

Elsewhere on Wednesday, markets were concerned by a real annual 17 percent surge in German plant and equipment orders, and by a stronger than forecast increase in U.S. durable goods orders, which was expected to drag on Treasuries.
Durable goods orders rose 1.8 percent in April against a economists' forecast of 1.3 percent.
The market is now looking ahead to U.S. jobless figures on Thursday, dealers said.
